legal.hook: by Shruti Awasthi* and Arpit Singh**
legal.summary: The article discusses a recent ruling under Section 144(1)(c) of the Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, concerning maintenance claims for major children based on 'mental injury.' The case involved a petition filed by a father seeking maintenance for his two adult children, aged 18 and 21, who claimed psychological distress due to their parents' separation. The court recognized that mental injury could warrant maintenance claims, setting a precedent for similar future cases. The judgment emphasized the importance of addressing emotional and psychological needs in maintenance disputes, thereby expanding the scope of what constitutes 'necessities' under the law. The ruling may influence how courts assess maintenance claims in the context of familial relationships and mental health considerations. The father was ordered to pay a monthly maintenance amount of ₹15,000 for each child, highlighting the court's commitment to ensuring the welfare of children beyond mere financial support.
legal.contextNote: This ruling is grounded in Section 144(1)(c) of the Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which allows for maintenance claims based on mental injury. legal.headline: Supreme Court’s new sequencing of matters in cause list: fresh and early-hearing matters in Part A, after-notice in Part B

legal.summary: The Supreme Court of India has revised its cause list arrangement, now publishing it in two parts. Part A will include fresh and early-hearing matters, while Part B will contain after-notice matters. This change ends the previous practice of assigning a sequence to matters at 10:30 a.m. The Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) has communicated this update, indicating a significant shift in how cases will be prioritized and heard moving forward. The new system aims to streamline the hearing process and improve the efficiency of case management in the Supreme Court.
legal.contextNote: This change in the Supreme Court's cause list arrangement reflects an effort to enhance judicial efficiency, potentially impacting case management under the Supreme Court Rules, 2013. (1) In-house counsel should monitor how this new sequencing affects the scheduling of their pending cases, especially those that may now be categorized as fresh matters.
